title: Notes, synthesis and literature reviews
note: Summary reports what one source says; synthesis puts several sources in conversation to show patterns, agreements, conflicts and gaps. Take notes in your own words with the citation attached, mark exact quotes clearly, and organize a literature review by theme, not source by source.

read.title: From pile to pattern
text: After a few weeks of searching, many students have a folder of PDFs and a draft that reads like a book report: Smith found this, Jones found that, Lee found something else. Each paragraph summarizes one source. The reader is left to do the real work of figuring out what it all means.

A literature review is supposed to do that work. Synthesis means putting sources in conversation. Instead of one paragraph per study, you write one paragraph per idea: "Three small trials reported improved sleep, but the largest trial found no effect, possibly because it used a shorter program." That sentence draws on several sources, notes a disagreement, and offers an explanation.

Good notes make this easier. Write notes in your own words, attach the citation to each one, and put any copied wording in quotation marks with a page number. A synthesis matrix, a grid with sources as rows and themes as columns, shows at a glance which sources address which question and where they agree.
Finally, notice what is missing. The gaps you find, such as untested groups, weak designs, or unanswered questions, often become the justification for your own research.

q.q: What is wrong with a review that has one paragraph per source?
o: It uses the wrong citation style
It leaves the reader to work out what the sources mean together

q.q: What does a synthesis matrix show?
o: The order in which you read sources

q.q: According to the reading, what often justifies new research?
o: Gaps found in the existing literature
